name: Follicular unit extraction (FUE)

card.summary: Hair transplant method that removes follicles one by one from the donor scalp, avoiding a linear scar at the cost of longer surgery.
card.aka: FUE, follicular unit excision, FOX procedure
card.note: Results depend on the surgeon; ongoing native hair loss may require further procedures.

quick.overview:
Follicular unit extraction is a hair transplant technique in which small circular punches remove individual follicular units, usually one to four hairs, from the back and sides of the scalp. They are then implanted in thinning or bald areas.

It was introduced in the early 2000s as an alternative to strip harvesting (FUT), which leaves a linear scar. Descriptions in the literature cite tiny scattered scars instead, though outcomes depend on technique and patient.
quick.mechanism: Grafts taken from the donor zone keep their genetic resistance to pattern hair loss, a principle called donor dominance, so transplanted hair is described as long-lasting. Extraction is done under local anaesthetic, with grafts placed into small recipient incisions.
quick.risks: Described effects include temporary swelling, temporary shedding of transplanted hair (shock loss), folliculitis, numbness, transected follicles and, in rare cases, scarring. Over-harvesting can leave a thinned donor area, and native hair loss can continue after surgery.

lead: Follicular unit extraction (FUE) is a hair restoration technique in which individual follicular units are removed from the donor scalp with small punches, instead of excising a strip of skin, and transplanted to areas of hair loss [1][2]. People use it to restore a lost hairline, add density to thinning crowns and temples, and fill scars or sparse eyebrows and beards, which changes how framed and youthful the face looks. The term was coined in a 2002 paper that introduced the approach as minimally invasive surgery for hair transplantation [1].

Wikipedia describes FUE as using 0.6 to 1.0 mm punches under local anaesthesia, leaving small scattered scars rather than a linear one, with recovery reported at under seven days, while noting drawbacks of longer surgery time, higher cost, candidacy restrictions and a steep learning curve [2]. Robotic systems have been developed to assist, with US approvals reported for NeoGraft in 2009 and ARTAS in 2011 [2].

A 2025 review of hair transplant literature from 2019 to 2024, covering 1,030 abstracts, described FUE and linear strip excision as the two state-of-the-art harvesting methods and reported improved aesthetic results from careful hairline design and concurrent medical management [3]. FUE is a major topic in hair loss and hairline discussions, including variants such as sapphire FUE and DHI.

paras: The donor area, typically the back and sides of the scalp, is usually shaved short, and punches of roughly 0.7 to 1.2 mm extract units of one to four hairs; grafts are stored in chilled solution and implanted into recipient sites made with fine needles or blades [4]. A session is described as commonly yielding 1,500 to 3,000 grafts [4].

The comparison technique is follicular unit transplantation from a strip (FUT), in which a strip of scalp is removed and dissected under microscopes into grafts, leaving a thin linear scar usually hidden by hair, with recovery of about two weeks and sutures or staples to remove unless subcuticular closure is used [2]. Reviews describe the choice of FUE versus elliptical strip harvesting, and manual versus robotic FUE, as a continuing controversy in hair transplantation [5].

A review describes robotic hair transplantation as allowing precise, efficient removal of follicular units and minimally invasive surgery, while stating that it does not replace candidate selection, hairline design or judgement about where to place hair [6]. The ARTAS system was approved in 2011, and a controlled study of 24 patients evaluated a capability added to the robot to harvest follicular units chosen by the number of hairs they contain, aiming to increase hair per wound [7]. A 2025 review says new devices have been developed for both extraction and insertion of units [3].

Scalp flaps and free grafts date to the 19th century, Okuda reported work in Japan in the 1930s, and Norman Orentreich's late-1950s work established donor dominance, the principle that transplanted hair keeps the characteristics of the donor site [2][3]. Walter Unger defined the safe donor zone, and strip harvesting replaced plugs in the 1980s [2].

Grokipedia credits Masumi Inaba with a manual follicular extraction approach in 1988, and reports that John Cole introduced smaller punches in the early 2000s [4]. The 2002 Rassman and colleagues paper presented the FOX procedure as a response to donor scarring from strip excision [1]. In 2017 the ISHRS reportedly favoured the term follicular unit excision [4]. Beard and other facial hair reconstruction have since become an area of practice [8].

Grokipedia reports new growth at three to four months and full results at 12 to 18 months, with graft survival of 85 to 95 percent, and lists edema, sterile folliculitis, numbness, transection and rare infection or hypertrophic scarring as complications [4]. These figures come from an AI-generated source and have not been independently verified. Wikipedia lists shock loss, usually temporary thinning, as the main side effect, and notes some surgeons report a lower proportion of successfully transplanted follicles than with FUT [2]. Postoperative numbness, itching and pain in the donor area are linked to delayed wound healing [9].

Wikipedia reports cost depends on graft numbers, citing about US$1.07 per graft in Turkey to US$7.00 in Canada, and UK totals ranging from 1,000 to 30,000 pounds [2]. Grokipedia gives broader per-graft ranges and says insurance rarely covers it [4].

The founding 2002 paper introduced FUE as an alternative to strip surgery, aimed at avoiding linear donor scars [1]. A bilateral controlled study of 24 patients assessed robotic selection of grafts by hair count [7]. A randomised controlled trial tested hair follicular-derived microtissue for donor-site wound healing and postoperative complications after FUE [9], and a registered 100-participant trial examined the same product for donor-site healing [10]. Other randomised trials examined tumescent solution with ropivacaine for postoperative pain in follicular unit excision [11], FUE with or without platelet-rich plasma in cicatricial alopecia [12], and de-epithelialization and graft survival [13].

Registered trials include one on wound dressings after FUE (n=25) [14], one of topical rifamycin SV for wound healing after sapphire FUE (n=70) [15], and a planned study of a protocol to maximise follicle survival (n=30) [16].

timeline.event: Okuda reports hair transplant work in Japan, per Wikipedia.[2]
Norman Orentreich's work establishes donor dominance.[2]
Masumi Inaba described manual follicular extraction, per Grokipedia.[4]
Rassman and colleagues published the FUE procedure.[1]
NeoGraft receives FDA approval, per Wikipedia.[2]
ISHRS reportedly renames the procedure follicular unit excision, per Grokipedia.[4]

lore.intro: FUE is regularly raised in hair-loss discussions as the transplant option, including on T Nation as long ago as 2008.[17]

claims.claim: FUE is the best solution once hair loss progresses
claims.believers: A 2008 T Nation poster called FUE the best solution 'when the time comes' for slowly progressing hair loss.[17]
claims.experts: Reviews describe FUE and strip excision as both state of the art, with continuing debate about the best harvesting method.[3][5]

chain: Individual follicular units are harvested from the donor scalp
Units are implanted in thinning or bald areas
Transplanted hair keeps its donor characteristics and grows in its new location
angle.text: FUE moves hair from the back and sides of the scalp, where hair tends to persist, to recipient areas. The result is a framed forehead and fuller coverage, and small punctate donor scars make short haircuts possible, which is one reason people choose it over strip harvesting.
